An interactive, bottom-up explainer

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash,
component by component

From RMSNorm to a 552B multimodal causal encoder–decoder
that keeps 890 bytes of global KV cache per token.
Primary source: DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression, arXiv:2609.19969 (Sep 2026).
Direct references: DeepSeek-V4 (arXiv:2606.19348) · mHC (arXiv:2512.24880) · DeepSeek-V3 (arXiv:2412.19437) · Engram (arXiv:2601.07372) · DSpark (arXiv:2607.05147).
Every diagram is live: drag, hover, slide. Press → to advance, Esc for the overview.
Motivation V4.1 §1

Long-horizon agents are input-heavy: the bottleneck moves to the KV cache

Agent loops re-send growing contexts (tool calls, files, screenshots). Sparse attention (V3.2, V4) already made long-context compute cheap; what remains:

  • Prefill compute on cache misses — every tool call is a new prefill.
  • Runtime KV in HBM — dominated by the global KV once contexts are long.
  • Persistent KV on SSD / host memory for prefix reuse, plus the I/O bandwidth to move it.

V4.1-Flash attacks all three jointly — architecture (CED, CSA2), precision (FP4 KV) and deployment (SWA bounded replay).

Plan of this deck: explain every component — even textbook ones — with its equation and a live diagram, then zoom out step by step until we reach the paper’s full architecture figure.

PART 1

Textbook atoms

The standard pieces every modern LLM is made of — explained once, precisely, so the DeepSeek-specific parts can be read as small deltas.

Atom 1 · Tokens and embeddings textbook

Text becomes a sequence of integer ids, ids become rows of a table

A tokenizer maps text to ids \(x_1,\dots,x_n\in\{1..V\}\). The embedding is a lookup, i.e. a one-hot times a matrix:

$$\mathbf h^{(0)}_t = E[x_t] = \mathbf 1_{x_t}^\top E,\qquad E\in\mathbb R^{V\times d}$$

At the top, a prediction head maps the last hidden state back to the vocabulary; training minimises next-token cross-entropy:

$$p(\cdot\mid x_{\le t})=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf h^{(L)}_tW_{\text{out}}),\quad \mathcal L_{\text{LM}}=-\tfrac1T\textstyle\sum_t\log p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t})$$

V4.1 trains \(E\), \(W_{\text{out}}\) and the Engram tables with a Sinkhorn-balanced momentum update instead of Adam (Part 2). The tokenizer here is a toy splitter.

Atom 2 · RMSNorm Zhang & Sennrich 2019 · used everywhere in V3/V4/V4.1

Normalisation rescales a vector to a fixed RMS — no mean subtraction

$$\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\mathbf x)=\mathbf g\odot\frac{\mathbf x}{\sqrt{\frac1d\sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2+\epsilon}}$$
  • Cheaper than LayerNorm (one reduction), same stabilising effect.
  • Used as pre-norm before each attention/MoE block, on queries and KV entries right before attention (bounds the logits → no QK-clip needed with Muon), inside the mHC coefficient predictor, and in Engram’s gate.
  • Because of it, the V4.1 main-KV latent satisfies \(\|\mathbf x\|_2\lesssim\sqrt{512}\approx 22.6\) — which is why FP4 needs no global scale.

Drag the input bars; toggle LayerNorm to see the extra mean-centering.

Atom 3 · Low-rank factorisation textbook · MLA, CSA queries, DSpark Markov head

Many DeepSeek tricks are “go through a narrow latent”

A \(d\times d'\) matrix of rank \(r\) factors as \(W=W^{D}W^{U}\): parameters and FLOPs drop from \(dd'\) to \(r(d+d')\). Truncated SVD gives the best rank-\(r\) approximation (Eckart–Young).

$$\mathbf c^Q_t=\mathbf h_tW^{DQ},\quad \mathbf q_t=\mathbf c^Q_tW^{UQ},\quad \mathbf q^I_t=\mathbf c^Q_tW^{IUQ}$$
  • Queries of CSA/CSA2: \(d\to d_c=1280\to n_hc=32768\); the latent is shared with the indexer queries.
  • MLA (V2/V3): keys/values through a cached 512-d latent.
  • Grouped output projection, DSpark Markov head (\(V\times V\) matrix at rank 256).
Atom 4 · Softmax textbook

Softmax turns scores into a distribution

$$\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf z)_j=\frac{e^{z_j/\tau}}{\sum_k e^{z_k/\tau}}$$
  • Invariant to adding a constant: only differences of logits matter (we subtract \(\max z\) for numerical stability).
  • Used for attention weights, next-token probabilities, the KV compressor weights \(S=\operatorname{softmax}(Z+B)\), DSpark draft distributions.
  • Its sigmoid cousin \(\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})\) appears in mHC (\(A_l=\sigma(\cdot)\)), Engram gates and DSpark confidences.

Drag the logits. Later we will add an attention sink to this same widget.

Atom 5 · Causal scaled dot-product attention Vaswani et al. 2017

Each token reads a weighted average of the previous tokens

$$\mathbf q_t=\mathbf h_tW^Q,\ \ \mathbf k_j=\mathbf h_jW^K,\ \ \mathbf v_j=\mathbf h_jW^V$$ $$\mathbf o_t=\sum_{j\le t}\operatorname{softmax}_j\!\Big(\frac{\mathbf q_t^\top\mathbf k_j}{\sqrt{d_h}}\Big)\mathbf v_j$$
  • Causal mask: \(j\le t\) — a token never sees the future.
  • Multi-head: \(n_h\) independent (q,k,v) triples, outputs concatenated then projected by \(W^O\).
  • Decoding one token costs \(O(t)\) and needs all past \(\mathbf k_j,\mathbf v_j\): the KV cache.

Hover a token to make it the query; switch heads to see different learned patterns (toy scores).

Atom 6 · Rotary position embedding (RoPE) Su et al. 2021 · partial RoPE in V4/V4.1

Positions as rotations: dot products depend only on the offset

Split a vector into 2-D pairs; rotate pair \(i\) at position \(m\) by angle \(m\theta_i\), \(\theta_i=b^{-2i/d_R}\):

$$\langle R_m\mathbf q, R_n\mathbf k\rangle=\langle\mathbf q,R_{n-m}\mathbf k\rangle$$
  • Partial RoPE: V4/V4.1 rotate only the last 64 of the 512 dims of queries and KV entries.
  • Since a KV entry is both key and value, the attention output inherits absolute rotations; V4 fixes this by rotating each head output with position \(-t\): the output then carries relative position.
$$\mathbf o_{t,i}\leftarrow \operatorname{RoPE}_{-t}(\mathbf o_{t,i})\ \text{ on the last 64 dims}$$
Atom 7 · What goes in the KV cache MHA · GQA · MQA · MLA (V2/V3) · shared-KV MQA (V4)

The KV cache layout is the first lever: bytes per token per layer

  • MHA: every head caches its own K and V.
  • GQA / MQA: heads share K,V (8 groups / 1).
  • MLA (V3): cache a 512-d latent \(\mathbf c^{KV}_t=\mathbf h_tW^{DKV}\) + a 64-d RoPE key; up-projections are absorbed into \(W^Q, W^O\).
  • Shared-KV MQA (V4, V4.1): a single 512-d entry \(C_t\) that is both the key and the value of every head.
$$\mathbf o_{t,i}=\operatorname{CoreAttn}\big(\mathbf q_{t,i},\ \mathcal K_t,\ \mathcal K_t\big)$$

This is only the entry-size axis. V4 adds the sequence axis (compression) and V4.1 the layer axis (sharing).

Atom 8 · Gated feed-forward (SwiGLU) with clamping Shazeer 2020 · clamp from gpt-oss, τ = 10 in V4/V4.1

Every expert is a small SwiGLU MLP — clamped to avoid activation blow-ups

$$\operatorname{FFN}(\mathbf u)=\big(\operatorname{SiLU}(\mathbf uW_1)\odot \mathbf uW_3\big)W_2,\qquad\operatorname{SiLU}(x)=x\,\sigma(x)$$

With clamping at \(\tau=10\) (gate capped above, linear branch clipped to \([-\tau,\tau]\)) the product stays bounded — important for low-precision (FP8/FP4) training and inference.

Sizes in V4.1: \(W_1,W_3\in\mathbb R^{5120\times2304}\), \(W_2\in\mathbb R^{2304\times5120}\): 35.4M params per expert.

Atom 9 · Pre-norm residual stream He et al. 2016

The residual stream is the model’s “bus” — mHC will widen it

$$\mathbf x_{l+1}=\mathbf x_l+\mathcal F_l\big(\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\mathbf x_l)\big)$$
  • Unrolled: \(\mathbf x_L=\mathbf x_0+\sum_l\mathcal F_l(\cdot)\): every block reads from and writes to a shared stream.
  • The identity path gives \(\partial\mathbf x_L/\partial\mathbf x_l=I+\dots\): stable signal and gradient propagation in depth.
  • In V4.1 each attention layer and each MoE layer is one \(\mathcal F_l\) (80 residual blocks).
Hyper-Connections replace the single stream by \(n\) streams and the fixed “+” by learned mixing — at the cost of losing the identity property, which mHC restores.
PART 2

DeepSeek building blocks

Mixture-of-experts, load balancing without auxiliary losses, manifold-constrained hyper-connections, and the optimizers that train them.

Block 1 · DeepSeekMoE V3 §2.1.2 · V4 §2.1 · V4.1 §2.1

Fine-grained routed experts + an always-on shared expert

$$\mathbf h'_t=\mathbf u_t+\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\operatorname{FFN}^{(s)}_i(\mathbf u_t)+\sum_{i=1}^{N_r}g_{i,t}\operatorname{FFN}^{(r)}_i(\mathbf u_t)$$ $$g_{i,t}=\frac{g'_{i,t}}{\sum_jg'_{j,t}},\quad g'_{i,t}=\begin{cases}s_{i,t}&s_{i,t}\in\operatorname{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}\},K_r)\\0&\text{else}\end{cases}$$
  • Affinity: \(s_{i,t}=\sigma(\mathbf u_t^\top\mathbf e_i)\) in V3, \(\sqrt{\operatorname{softplus}(\mathbf u_t^\top\mathbf e_i)}\) since V4.
  • V4.1: every layer is MoE (no dense layers), 1 shared + 384 routed, 6 active — the experts hold almost all 552B parameters while only ~7/385 of them run per token.
Block 2 · Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing V3 §2.1.2 · V4.1 §2.1.1 (per-modality biases)

Balance experts with a routing-only bias, not with a loss

$$g'_{i,t}=\begin{cases}s_{i,t}& s_{i,t}+b_i\in\operatorname{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}+b_j\},K_r)\\0&\text{else}\end{cases}$$ $$b_i\leftarrow b_i+\gamma\operatorname{sign}(\bar c-c_i)\ \ \text{after each step}$$
  • The bias changes who is selected, never the gate value → no gradient interference.
  • V4.1: text and image tokens prefer different experts, so it keeps two bias vectors, one per modality (γ = 0.001 each).
  • A tiny sequence-wise loss guards against extreme imbalance inside one sequence (weight \(10^{-4}\)):
$$\mathcal L_{\text{Bal}}=\alpha\sum_{i}f_iP_i,\ \ f_i=\tfrac{N_r}{K_rT}\textstyle\sum_t\mathbb 1(i\in\text{Top}_t),\ P_i=\tfrac1T\sum_t\tfrac{s_{i,t}}{\sum_js_{j,t}}$$
Block 3 · Hyper-Connections (HC) Zhu et al. 2024 · mHC §3

Widen the residual stream to \(n\) streams with learned read / write / mix

$$X_{l+1}=B_lX_l+C_l\,\mathcal F_l(A_lX_l)$$
  • \(A_l\) (pre, \(1\times n\)): reads a \(d\)-dim input from \(n\) streams.
  • \(B_l\) (res, \(n\times n\)): mixes the streams — the ablation shows it gives most of the gain.
  • \(C_l\) (post, \(n\times 1\)): writes the block output back.
  • The inner layer still sees width \(d\): extra cost is tiny (\(n=4\ll d\)).
Unconstrained \(B_l\) breaks the identity mapping: products \(\prod_lB_l\) can explode or vanish over 80 blocks → loss spikes at scale.
Block 4 · Manifold-constrained HC (mHC) mHC §4 · V4 §2.2

Project \(B_l\) onto doubly-stochastic matrices with Sinkhorn–Knopp

$$B_l\in\mathcal M=\{M\ge0,\ M\mathbf 1_n=\mathbf 1_n,\ \mathbf 1_n^\top M=\mathbf 1_n^\top\}$$
  • \(\|B_l\|_2\le1\): non-expansive, forward and backward.
  • \(\mathcal M\) is closed under products: the composite map over any depth stays in \(\mathcal M\).
  • \(\mathcal M\) is the Birkhoff polytope: convex hull of permutations → \(B_l\) is a soft routing between streams. \(n=1\) recovers the plain residual.
$$M^{(0)}=\exp(\tilde B_l),\quad M^{(t)}=\mathcal T_r(\mathcal T_c(M^{(t-1)})),\quad B_l=M^{(20)}$$

Right chart: 60 random layers. Unconstrained products drift by orders of magnitude; projected ones keep gain exactly 1.

Block 4b · mHC dynamic parameterisation V4 §2.2 · mHC §4.2

Coefficients are predicted per token from all \(n\) streams

Flatten and normalise the streams, then produce dynamic + static parts:

$$\hat X_l=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\operatorname{vec}(X_l))\in\mathbb R^{1\times nd}$$ $$\begin{aligned}\tilde A_l&=\alpha^{\rm pre}_l\,(\hat X_lW^{\rm pre}_l)+S^{\rm pre}_l\\ \tilde B_l&=\alpha^{\rm res}_l\operatorname{Mat}(\hat X_lW^{\rm res}_l)+S^{\rm res}_l\\ \tilde C_l&=\alpha^{\rm post}_l\,(\hat X_lW^{\rm post}_l)^\top+S^{\rm post}_l\end{aligned}$$

then constrain:

$$A_l=\sigma(\tilde A_l),\qquad C_l=2\sigma(\tilde C_l),\qquad B_l=\operatorname{SinkhornKnopp}(\tilde B_l)$$
  • \(W^{\rm pre},W^{\rm post}\in\mathbb R^{nd\times n}\), \(W^{\rm res}\in\mathbb R^{nd\times n^2}\): with \(n=4,d=5120\) that is only \(20480\times24\) weights per block.
  • Gates \(\alpha\) start small → each block starts close to a fixed static mixing.
  • Non-negative \(A_l, C_l\): no signal cancellation between streams.
  • The normalisation weights are folded into \(W\) offline, and the RMS division is applied after the projection — this is what makes the single-pass kernel possible (next slide).
V4.1 keeps \(n_{hc}=4\), 20 Sinkhorn iterations, and even integrates Engram with mHC: one shared value projection, one key projection per stream.
Block 5 · Single-Pass mHC & Mega-mHC kernel V4.1 §2.4.1 (new)

Shift the input mixing by one block → the residual is read once

V4 executes three dependent kernels per block:

$$\begin{aligned}X_l&=B_{l-1}X_{l-1}+C_{l-1}Y_{l-1}&&\text{(over } n)\\(A_l,B_l,C_l)&=\mathcal H(X_l)&&\text{(over } nd)\\\hat X_l&=A_lX_l&&\text{(needs } A_l!)\end{aligned}$$

V4.1 uses the previous block’s \(A\):

$$X_{l+1}=B_lX_l+C_l\,\mathcal F_l(A_{l-1}X_l)$$

Now each tile of \(X_l\) is updated, mixed and accumulated into \(\mathcal H\) in one sweep. Traffic: \((4n{+}4)d\to(2n{+}2)d\) — the lower bound — with “negligible” quality loss.

Block 6 · Muon optimizer (hybrid Newton–Schulz, head-wise) V4 §2.4 · V4.1 §2.5

Muon: orthogonalise the momentum, i.e. push all singular values to 1

$$\begin{aligned}M_t&=\mu M_{t-1}+G_t\\O_t&=\operatorname{NS}_{10}(\mu M_t+G_t)\cdot\sqrt{\max(n,m)}\,\gamma\\W_t&=W_{t-1}(1-\eta\lambda)-\eta O_t\end{aligned}$$
  • NS acts on singular values: \(\sigma\mapsto a\sigma+b\sigma^3+c\sigma^5\). 8 fast steps, then 2 steps with \((2,-1.5,0.5)\) that pin \(\sigma\) at exactly 1.
  • \(\gamma=0.18\) matches AdamW’s update RMS; momentum 0.95, weight decay 0.1.
  • V4.1: head-wise Muon for Q and K — each head gets its own preconditioner.
  • AdamW stays for norms, biases, gates.
Block 7 · Sinkhorn-balanced updates for embeddings, head & Engram V4.1 §2.5, Alg. 1 (new)

For huge token×feature tables: balance rows and columns of the update

Muon’s recipe with Newton–Schulz replaced by Sinkhorn normalisation of the Nesterov momentum \(\widehat G_t\):

$$\Delta_t=\sqrt n\,D_r\widehat G_tD_c,\qquad W_{t+1}=W_t-\gamma\eta_t\Delta_t$$
  • Alternate \(K=11\) row / column \(\ell_2\) normalisations → every token row and feature column gets RMS ≈ 1.
  • Rows with tiny gradient (unseen tokens / n-grams) are masked.
  • Only one momentum buffer — vs Adam’s two — on the 196B-parameter Engram tables. Empirically better than Adam.
PART 3

Long-context attention

From sliding windows to compressed sparse attention, and V4.1’s cross-layer sharing that brings the global KV cache to 890 bytes per token.

Framing V4.1 §2.3

KV cost = entry size × number of entries per layer × number of layers

① Entry size

GQA / MQA fewer KV heads; MLA a small shared latent; V4 one 512-d entry used as K and V; V4.1 stores it in FP4.

$$\text{bytes}(C_t)=512\cdot\tfrac12+\tfrac{512}{16}=288$$

② Sequence

Compress every \(m\) tokens into one entry (CSA: \(m{=}4\), HCA: \(m'{=}128\) in V4) and let each query read only the top-\(k\) entries.

$$\#\text{entries}=n/m,\quad\text{read }k=512$$

③ Layers

Let layers reuse another layer’s KV and Top-K indices (CLA, IndexCache, YOCO…). V4.1’s CSA2 does ①+②+③ jointly.

$$40\text{ layers}\to 4\text{ KV producers}$$
Local detail is handled separately by a sliding window in every layer, whose cache is bounded (\(n_{\text{win}}=128\)) and independent of context length. So for long contexts the global KV dominates — that is what V4.1 compresses.
Attention 1 · Sliding-window attention (SWA) Longformer/Mistral · every V4/V4.1 layer

Local attention: a fixed window, a growing receptive field

$$\mathbf o_i=\sum_{j=i-n_{\rm win}+1}^{i}\operatorname{softmax}_j\Big(\tfrac{\mathbf q_i^\top\mathbf k_j}{\sqrt d}\Big)\mathbf v_j$$
  • Cache per layer: \(n_{\rm win}\) entries, whatever the context length.
  • Stacking \(l\) layers gives a receptive field of \(l(n_{\rm win}-1)+1\) tokens.
  • V4.1: the first two encoder layers are pure SWA; every other layer adds an SWA branch next to its global (CSA2) branch. SWA KV stays FP8 — it is quantisation-sensitive.

That stacking property matters later: exactly rebuilding the SWA state needs \(L\cdot n_{\rm win}\) tokens — “bounded replay” cuts this to \(n_{\rm win}\).

Attention 2 · Token-level KV compressor V4 §2.3.1–2.3.2 · V4.1 §2.3

Compress \(m\) tokens into one KV entry with learned softmax weights

$$C=HW^{KV},\qquad Z=HW^{Z}\qquad(\in\mathbb R^{n\times c})$$

Per channel, a softmax over the tokens of a block decides how much each token contributes:

  • CSA (V4): two series \(a,b\); each entry pools \(2m\) tokens (its block + the previous one) with positional biases \(B^a,B^b\).
  • HCA (V4): one series, \(m'=128\): extreme compression, dense attention over all entries.
  • CSA2 (V4.1): no overlap, no positional bias, \(m=2\) (encoder) or \(m=1\) (decoder: no compression at all!).

Hover a compressed entry to see which tokens feed it and with what weights.

Attention 3 · Lightning indexer & top-k selection DSA (V3.2) · V4 §2.3.1

A tiny FP4 attention decides which \(k\) entries the real attention reads

$$\mathbf q^I_t=\mathbf c^Q_tW^{IUQ},\qquad \mathbf w^I_t=\mathbf h_tW^w$$ $$I_{t,s}=\sum_{h=1}^{n^I_h}w^I_{t,h}\operatorname{ReLU}\big(\mathbf q^I_{t,h}\cdot K^I_s\big)$$ $$\mathcal C_t=\{C_s\mid I_{t,s}\in\operatorname{Top\text{-}k}(I_{t,:})\},\ \ s<\lfloor t/m\rfloor$$
  • Still scans all entries, but with 32 heads × 128 dims in FP4: far cheaper than the 64 × 512 main attention.
  • Main attention then costs \(O(k+n_{\rm win})\) per token, independent of context length.
Attention 4 · Compressed Sparse Attention (V4), assembled V4 Fig. 3

CSA = compressor + indexer + top-k + SWA branch + shared-KV MQA

Attention 5 · The details that make it trainable V4 §2.3.3

Q/KV RMSNorm, partial RoPE, attention sink, grouped output projection

  • RMSNorm on every query head and on the KV entry before attention → bounded logits.
  • Partial RoPE on the last 64 dims, and \(\operatorname{RoPE}_{-t}\) on the outputs.
  • Attention sink: a learnable logit per head in the denominator lets a head put total weight < 1 (even ≈ 0) on real tokens:
$$s_{h,i,j}=\frac{e^{z_{h,i,j}}}{\sum_ke^{z_{h,i,k}}+e^{z'_h}}$$
  • Grouped output projection: \(n_hc=32768\) is too wide for one \(d\)-projection; project 8 groups of 8 heads to \(d_g=1024\) each, then \(8192\to d\).
Attention 6 · From V4’s hybrid to V4.1’s pure CSA2 V4 §2.3 · V4.1 §2.3

V4 interleaves CSA and HCA; V4.1 keeps one simplified mechanism

CSA (V4)HCA (V4)CSA2 (V4.1)
compression\(m=4\), overlapping \(2m\) sources, positional bias\(m'=128\), non-overlapping\(m=2\) enc / \(m=1\) dec, non-overlapping, no positional bias
selectionlightning indexer, top-\(k\)none (dense over \(n/128\) entries)indexer top-512, or reuse of another layer’s indices
indexer keysseparate compression path from \(H\)—projected from main KV
local branchSWA, \(n_{\rm win}=128\)SWA, \(n_{\rm win}=128\)SWA, \(n_{\rm win}=128\)
cross-layer——Full / Reindex / Reuse modes
main KV storageFP8 (448 dims) + BF16 (64 RoPE dims)sameFP4 E2M1 + E4M3 scale per 16

The V4.1 view: “V4 is an SWA local-processing backbone augmented with compressed global context” — so simplify the global branch and share it across layers, keep the local branch per layer.

Attention 7 · CSA2: cross-layer KV and index reuse V4.1 §2.3.1, Fig. 4

Three static modes decide what a layer computes and what it borrows

  • Full computes main KV (\(C_l=H_lW^{KV}_l\)), projects indexer K from it, runs its indexer → fresh Top-K.
  • Reindex reuses the latest main KV and indexer K; its own indexer Q re-scores them → fresh Top-K.
  • Reuse reuses main KV and the latest Top-K indices → straight to sparse attention.

In every mode the layer keeps its own query and own SWA KV, so each layer still produces a different output.

$$\text{enc: }[\text{SWA}]^2\,[\text{F}\,\text{U}^5]^3\qquad\text{dec: }[\text{F}\,\text{U}^3]\,[\text{R}\,\text{U}^3]^4$$
Attention 8 · Hierarchical Sparse Indexer V4.1 §2.3.2, Fig. 5 (decoder only, post-training)

The first decoder indexer narrows the search space of the later ones

  • The Full layer scores all positions (as usual) and picks its Top-512.
  • It also takes the max score per block of 8, keeps the best 2,048 blocks → a 16,384-position candidate pool.
  • Each Reindex layer scores only the pool: per-query indexer cost becomes constant in context length.
  • Trained with the same restriction, so deeper indexers learn under the search domain they will use.

Lower the “layer correlation” to see when a shared pool starts to miss what a deeper layer would have picked.

Attention 9 · FP4 main KV cache (QAT) V4.1 §2.4.4

4-bit KV entries, trained for: E2M1 with one E4M3 scale per 16 channels

  • Indexer Q/K were already FP4 (MXFP4) in V4 to speed up scoring. V4.1 extends QAT to the main KV cache — here FP4 saves storage; values are dequantised before attention.
  • NVFP4-like, minus the second-level global scale: RMSNorm + RoPE bound \(|x|\lesssim22.6\) (observed ≈ 10), far below \(448\times6\).
  • Quantised after RoPE; RoPE and non-RoPE dims share the format. SWA KV stays FP8.
$$\hat x=s\cdot\operatorname{E2M1}(x/s),\qquad s=\operatorname{E4M3}\big(\max_{16}|x|/6\big)$$
Attention 10 · Where 890 bytes per token comes from our reconstruction from V4.1 §4.2.1 — matches the paper’s 890 B

Only 4 of 40 layers produce global KV — and they store it in FP4

  • Encoder: 3 Full layers at \(m=2\) → \(3\times\tfrac12=1.5\) entries/token.
  • Decoder: 1 Full layer at \(m=1\) → 1 entry/token (Reindex layers reuse it).
  • Each entry: 288 B main KV (FP4) + 68 B indexer K (128-d MXFP4).
$$2.5\times(288+68)=890\ \text{B/token}$$

Toggle sharing / FP4 to see each factor: layer sharing alone is worth ≈ 12×. The V4-Flash bar is our estimate from its published configuration (ratio ≈ ¼ as reported). The SWA KV (constant ≈ 128 entries/layer) is not included.

Zoom-out checkpoint 1

An attention layer inside an mHC block

PART 4

Macro architecture

The causal encoder–decoder, bounded replay, conditional memory, speculative decoding and the vision pathway.

Macro 1 · Causal Encoder–Decoder (CED) V4.1 §2.2 · inspired by YOCO

The decoder’s global KV is projected from the encoder output

$$C_l=H_{L/2}W^{KV}_l,\qquad Z_l=H_{L/2}W^Z_l,\qquad l>\tfrac L2$$
  • Prefill of a prompt: run the 20 encoder layers on all tokens, then one matmul per decoder Full layer gives the decoder’s global KV. 8B active params / token instead of 16B.
  • SWA stays layer-local in every layer (more depth for local KV than YOCO) — so the decoder’s SWA KV for the last tokens must be replayed (next slide).
  • Decode: a new token runs all 40 layers (16B active).
$$\mathcal O(NL)\ \to\ \mathcal O\big(NL/2+n_{\rm win}L/2\big)\approx\mathcal O(NL/2)$$
Macro 2 · SWA bounded replay V4.1 §3.2.2

Rebuild the SWA state approximately from only the last \(n_{\rm win}\) tokens

  • Encoder replay: prefix cache hit on global KV, SWA KV evicted → replay the last \(n_{\rm win}\) cached tokens with the uncached suffix. Consequence: no SWA KV in the persistent cache (≈ ½ of it in V4).
  • Decoder replay: every prefill runs the decoder only on the last \(n_{\rm win}\) prompt tokens to create its SWA KV for decoding — never cached.
  • Approximate by design, “negligible” quality impact; the decoder replay is also simulated during post-training.
$$\text{persistent KV: }\underbrace{\tfrac12}_{\text{no SWA}}\times\underbrace{\tfrac14}_{\text{CSA2+FP4}}\approx\tfrac18\ \text{of V4-Flash}$$
Macro 3 · Engram conditional memory Engram (arXiv:2601.07372) · V4.1 §2.4.2

A 196B-parameter hashed n-gram lookup table, gated by context

  • Tokenizer compression \(\mathcal P:V\to V'\) (NFKC, lower-case…) then suffix n-grams \(g_{t,n}\), \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\).
  • Multi-head hashing: 8 heads per order, each into a table of prime size ≈ 16M; concatenate the rows.
  • Context-aware gate: the hidden state acts as a query against the memory’s key; wrong / colliding memories get \(\alpha_t\to0\).
  • V4.1 drops the short causal conv, uses FP8 tables, 2 modules (layers 1 and 14), Sinkhorn-balanced updates, 5× learning rate.

Addresses depend only on token ids → embeddings are prefetched from host memory over RDMA while earlier layers compute.

Macro 4 · DSpark speculative decoding DSpark (arXiv:2607.05147) · V4.1 §2.4.3

Draft 5 tokens in one pass, verify only what is worth verifying

  • Semi-autoregressive drafter: 3 Transformer blocks (window 128) produce 5 base logit vectors in parallel; a low-rank Markov head adds dependence on the previously drafted token.
  • Confidence head predicts per-position acceptance \(c_k\), trained on \(c_k^*=1-\tfrac12\|p^d_k-p^t_k\|_1\).
  • Scheduler: greedily admit draft tokens by survival \(a_{r,j}=\prod_{i\le j}c_{r,i}\) while expected throughput \(\Theta=\tau\cdot\mathrm{SPS}(B)\) grows.
  • Replaces V3/V4’s MTP; trained after pre-training on a frozen backbone, then alongside it (no gradient into the backbone).
Macro 5 · Vision pathway V4.1 §2.1.1

DeepSeek-ViT → 3×3 pixel-unshuffle → MLP → shared backbone

  • DeepSeek-ViT trained from scratch: 2D-RoPE (any resolution), linear patch embedding (Muon-friendly), RMSNorm, SwiGLU; SigLIP contrastive pre-training on ≈47B pairs, then autoregressive fine-tuning with a 4B MoE LLM.
  • Pixel-unshuffle 3×3: 9 neighbouring patch features concatenated along channels → 9× fewer tokens.
  • Visual tokens are inserted at image positions and processed by the same layers as text from the start of pre-training — with per-modality MoE balancing biases.

What each component buys

componentoriginwhat it reduces / improvesnumber to remember
DeepSeekMoE + loss-free balancing (per modality)V2 → V3 → V4.1active compute per parameter6+1 of 385 experts / layer
mHC → Single-Pass mHC (Mega-mHC)mHC → V4 → V4.1stable wide residual; activation traffic\((4n{+}4)d\to(2n{+}2)d\)
Muon (head-wise) + Sinkhorn-balanced updatesV4 → V4.1convergence; optimizer memory on tables1 buffer instead of 2
Shared-KV MQA, low-rank Q, grouped outputV4KV entry size, projection costone 512-d entry = K = V
Compressor + lightning indexer (CSA)V3.2 → V4entries per layer, attention readstop-512 + 128 window
CSA2 Full / Reindex / ReuseV4.1KV layers, indexer passes4 of 40 layers make KV
Hierarchical Sparse IndexerV4.1indexer cost in decoder16,384-position pool

Result: the global KV footprint is 890 B/token (≈ ¼ of V4-Flash), the persistent KV ≈ ⅛, decode FLOPs grow only ~¼ from 4K to 1M context — while the base model matches V4-Pro-Base with ⅓ of the total and ¼ of the active parameters.

Appendix · Training recipe V4.1 §4.2.2

How the 552B backbone was trained

  • 45T multimodal tokens, batch 100.6M tokens, no instabilities.
  • LR: warm-up 2000 steps → \(2.6\times10^{-4}\) until 28T → cosine to \(2.6\times10^{-5}\) at 40T → constant to 45T.
  • Sparse attention from scratch at 64K context (no dense warm-up); extended to 1M at 34T tokens.
  • Vision encoder frozen until LR decay, then unfrozen with a smaller LR.
  • MTP is dropped; DSpark trained afterwards. HSI and FP4 KV QAT introduced in post-training.
  • Muon (momentum 0.95, wd 0.1, RMS 0.18) for linear maps; head-wise for Q and K.
  • AdamW (\(\beta=(0.9,0.95)\), \(\epsilon=10^{-20}\), wd 0.1) for norms and non-matrix parameters.
  • Sinkhorn-balanced momentum (\(K=11,\tau=10^{-3}\)) for embeddings, head and Engram (5× LR).
  • Loss-free balancing: bias speed 0.001 per modality; sequence-wise loss weight \(10^{-4}\).
  • Post-training: standard SFT → RL → on-policy distillation; all changes are in the data pipeline.
